missions.label: Chapter 9
missions.title: Under the same roof
missions.subtitle: St. Michael’s · 1832
missions.summary: Search the kitchen, follow the horse, and uncover the gap between a master’s words and deeds.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Back in St. Michael’s, Thomas Auld kept us hungry. My sister Eliza, my aunt Priscilla, Henny, and I shared the kitchen. Food spoiled in storage while we went without.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Walk the kitchen and find the supplies. This search represents our struggle for food; the food locations are a game illustration.

stages.title: Meet Thomas by the meeting house

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Thomas attended a Methodist camp meeting in August 1832. I hoped religion would make him kinder. Instead, he became crueler and used scripture to defend abuse.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: He fed visiting preachers while we stayed hungry. Cookman showed sympathy. Wilson’s reading school was broken up after only three meetings.

task.title: Words and deeds
choices: He frees everyone in the kitchen.
He lets the reading school continue.
task.why: Douglass’s hope for kindness is disappointed. Religious profession does not change Thomas’s cruelty.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I let Thomas’s horse run away, so I could fetch it from William Hamilton’s farm. Hamilton gave people enough to eat. Getting food drove my decision.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Thomas sent me to Edward Covey for a year. Covey was known for breaking young enslaved people. That reputation let him get cheap labor.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I dreaded his cruelty, but was glad I would at least get enough to eat. Hunger had narrowed my choices.

missions.label: Chapter 10
missions.title: A voice unbroken
missions.subtitle: 1833–1835 and the return to Baltimore
missions.summary: Work the farm, stand your ground, teach a hidden class, plan together, and learn a trade in Baltimore.

stages.title: Gather the wood for the cart

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: On January first, 1833, I began work for Covey. I had never worked as a field hand. He sent me to fetch wood with unbroken oxen. The cart overturned; later the oxen smashed through a gate.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Covey punished me instead of teaching me. His constant work and surprise surveillance wore down my body and hope. We called his sneaking manner the snake.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: White sails moved freely across the Chesapeake. I spoke to those ships as I thought about my own captivity. My longing for freedom survived, even when I felt broken.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Covey’s religion did not make him just. He treated Caroline’s children as increased wealth. I describe cruelty reaching into work, family, and faith.

stages.title: Reach the woods after the collapse

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I collapsed in the summer heat while fanning wheat. Covey attacked me. I walked seven miles to ask Thomas for protection, but he ordered me back.

lines.speaker: Sandy Jenkins · retold
lines.text: I offered shelter and a root. I believed that carrying it on the right side would prevent a whipping. Frederick doubted me. The story reports my belief; it does not prove magic.

stages.title: Hold your ground in the stable

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: On Monday, Covey tried to tie me in the stable. I resisted. Hughes tried to help him, while Bill refused to help with the whipping. The struggle lasted nearly two hours.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Covey never whipped me again. The struggle restored confidence and my resolve to be free. It did not end my enslavement.

rhythm.title: Stand your ground
rhythm.caption: Hit the marked window four times. This timing challenge symbolizes resistance; it does not reenact the violence.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: After Covey, I worked for William Freeland. He gave enough food, proper meal time, and better tools. Still, I wanted to be my own master.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I taught Henry and John Harris and others to read. More than forty learners came to the Sabbath school. We risked punishment because knowledge mattered to us.

rhythm.title: Keep the lesson alive
rhythm.caption: Follow the chalk rhythm. Four successful beats complete the lesson.

stages.title: Gather the plan by the canoe

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: With Henry and John Harris, my uncle Henry Bailey, and Charles Roberts, I planned to travel up the Chesapeake by canoe, then follow the North Star beyond Maryland. Sandy withdrew from the attempt.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I wrote passes using William Hamilton’s name. Baltimore was a cover story for the Easter holiday. We wanted freedom and trusted each other.

task.title: Build the plan
task.instruction: Which is the group’s actual plan?
choices: Canoe up the bay, then travel north beyond Maryland.
Earn freedom by working for Covey.
Settle permanently in Baltimore using the passes.
task.why: Baltimore is written on the passes to disguise their real northward intention.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: We were arrested before leaving. I burned my pass. Henry ate his with a biscuit. We denied the plan and held together, but were taken to Easton jail.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: The others were taken home; I was left alone. Separation hurt most. Thomas eventually sent me back to Hugh in Baltimore, rather than sending me to Alabama.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: At William Gardner’s shipyard I faced constant conflicting orders. Four white apprentices attacked me. No white witness would testify, so the law gave me no protection.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Hugh moved me to Walter Price’s yard. I learned to caulk with mallet and irons and earned skilled wages. But every Saturday Hugh took every cent. Better conditions sharpened my desire for freedom.

rhythm.title: Seal the seam
rhythm.caption: Time four mallet strokes to the gold window.

missions.label: Chapter 11
missions.title: My own name
missions.subtitle: 1838–1841 · New York to New Bedford
missions.genre: Safe haven, harbor work & a public voice
missions.summary: Find allies, make a home, earn wages for yourself, and step forward to speak.

stages.title: Reach the end of the old contract

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Hugh let me hire my own time, but I had to pay him three dollars every week and meet my own expenses. When I returned late from a camp meeting, he took that arrangement away.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: On September third, 1838, I reached New York, free from the immediate grasp of slavery. I do not reveal the route or helpers. Naming them could endanger others.

task.title: Respect the silence
task.instruction: Why is the escape route missing from the Narrative?
choices: To protect helpers and future fugitives.
Because Douglass never reached New York.
Because Ruggles forbade him to write any book.
task.why: He deliberately withholds details that could teach enslavers how to intercept escaping people.

lines.speaker: David Ruggles · retold
lines.text: Frederick was alone and afraid of kidnapping. I gave him shelter and recommended New Bedford. With his caulking skills, he might find work there.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Anna Murray, already free, joined me. Reverend James Pennington married us on September fifteenth. Ruggles gave us five dollars and an introduction for the journey.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: In New Bedford, Nathan and Mrs. Johnson welcomed us. Nathan paid the stage fare so our baggage could be released. Their help made a new beginning possible.

lines.speaker: Nathan Johnson · retold
lines.text: There were many Johnsons in New Bedford. I had been reading The Lady of the Lake, and suggested Douglass. Frederick kept his first name to preserve his identity.

task.title: A name of my own
task.why: Nathan Johnson suggested Douglass, inspired by The Lady of the Lake.

stages.title: Carry the oil cargo to the wharf

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: New Bedford’s wealth challenged the idea that prosperity needed slavery. Working people had dignity, and the Black community protected one another.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: On my third day I loaded a sloop with oil. For the first time, earnings belonged to me and supported Anna and me. Racial prejudice still kept me from working as a caulker.

stages.title: Read the paper by the harbor

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I sawed wood, shoveled coal, cleaned chimneys, and moved oil casks. Nathan lent me a saw and a wood-horse. Free life required work, not dependence on an enslaver.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: About four months after arriving, I subscribed to The Liberator. Its anti-slavery message inspired me, and I attended meetings whenever I could.

rhythm.title: Make the work your own
rhythm.caption: Keep four strokes in time. Your work now supports your own household.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: At an anti-slavery convention in Nantucket on August eleventh, 1841, William C. Coffin urged me to speak. I hesitated before a white audience, then began to find my voice.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: From that time until now, I have spoken for the cause of my brethren. The Narrative ends this journey with public advocacy, not the end of my life.

rhythm.title: Take the floor
rhythm.caption: Meet the four cues. Build momentum and finish your first address.

missions.label: Appendix
missions.title: Truth, love, justice
missions.subtitle: The closing argument · 1845
missions.summary: Expose the contradiction between belief and behavior, then carry Douglass’s closing pledge forward.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I am not condemning every religion. I distinguish the Christianity of Christ from the slaveholding religion of America. I love a pure, peaceable, impartial faith.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Someone who praises family while selling families apart contradicts that faith. The same is true of demanding Bible reading while denying people literacy.

task.title: Separate the claim
task.why: He explicitly distinguishes Christianity proper from religious institutions that support slavery.

stages.title: Bring the contradictions into the light

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I describe slave trading and church institutions supporting each other. Outward rituals cannot excuse neglecting justice, mercy, and faith. My criticism includes complicit churches north and south.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I copy a parody attributed to a northern Methodist preacher. It sets pious words beside cruel deeds, exposing their contradiction through satire.

task.title: Hear the irony
task.instruction: Why does the parody repeat heavenly union?
choices: To expose the hypocrisy of piety joined to cruelty.
To praise slaveholders for consistent kindness.
To describe the successful escape route.
task.why: The praise is ironic: the repeated phrase clashes with kidnapping, theft, and abuse.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: I hope this book throws light on slavery and hastens deliverance. I rely on truth, love, and justice, and pledge myself anew to the cause.

lines.speaker: Frederick Douglass · retold
lines.text: Frederick Douglass signs this closing statement in Lynn, Massachusetts, on April twenty-eighth, 1845. His story asks us to see clearly and judge words by actions.

rhythm.title: A voice carried forward
rhythm.caption: Finish four beats to carry the closing pledge into the light.

questions.prompt: What dominates Douglass’s experience under Thomas Auld?
questions.explanation: Food spoiled in storage while the enslaved kitchen workers went hungry.

questions.prompt: Which two relatives share the kitchen with Douglass?
choices: Eliza, his sister, and Priscilla, his aunt.
Anna, his wife, and Nathan, his uncle.
Sophia, his sister, and Henny, his mother.
questions.explanation: He names Eliza and Priscilla, along with Henny and himself.

questions.prompt: How does Thomas’s conversion affect his behavior?
choices: He becomes crueler and uses scripture to justify it.
questions.explanation: Douglass hoped for kindness; Thomas instead became more cruel.

questions.prompt: Which preacher shows sympathy toward enslaved people?
questions.explanation: Cookman’s sympathy gave enslaved people hope; Douglass distinguishes him from other visitors.

questions.prompt: What happens to Wilson’s reading school?
choices: It is broken up after three meetings.
It becomes a paid trade school.
questions.explanation: West, Fairbanks, and others forcibly break up the school.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass let the horse run to Hamilton’s farm?
choices: He can retrieve it and get food there.
He wants to sell the horse in New York.
He has permission to escape by canoe.
questions.explanation: Hamilton gave enslaved people enough food; the horse gave Douglass a reason to visit.

questions.prompt: Why is Covey able to obtain cheap labor?
choices: His reputation for breaking young enslaved people.
He pays the highest caulking wages.
He offers legal freedom after a year.
questions.explanation: Enslavers value his reputation for enforcing submission.

questions.prompt: Why is Douglass partly glad to leave for Covey?
choices: He will receive his own wages.
questions.explanation: Hunger makes sufficient food a powerful attraction despite Covey’s cruelty.

questions.prompt: What does Thomas’s treatment of Henny expose?
choices: Cruelty toward a disabled enslaved woman.
questions.explanation: Henny’s hands were injured by childhood burns; Thomas abused and ultimately abandoned her.

questions.prompt: Where does Chapter IX chiefly take place?
questions.explanation: Douglass returns from Baltimore to Thomas Auld at St. Michael’s in March 1832.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong on Douglass’s first wood-gathering trip for Covey?
choices: Unbroken oxen overturn the cart and later wreck a gate.
questions.explanation: He has no field experience and struggles to control the untrained oxen.

questions.prompt: Why do workers call Covey the snake?
choices: He sneaks up and spies on them.
He sails secretly to New York.
questions.explanation: Covey hides, crawls through fields, and pretends to leave to catch workers by surprise.

questions.prompt: What do the white sails on the Chesapeake represent to Douglass?
choices: A completed escape to New York.
questions.explanation: His address to the ships expresses longing and renewed determination.

questions.prompt: What does Thomas do when Douglass asks for protection from Covey?
questions.explanation: After the heat collapse and attack, Douglass walks seven miles seeking help, but Thomas refuses it.

questions.prompt: How should Sandy’s root be understood?
choices: A belief Sandy presents, which Douglass initially doubts.
questions.explanation: The account reports Sandy’s belief; it does not establish magic as fact.

questions.prompt: What is the main consequence of resisting Covey?
choices: Restored confidence and no further whippings from Covey.
A successful canoe escape that day.
questions.explanation: The struggle restores Douglass’s spirit while he remains enslaved.

questions.prompt: Who refuses to help Covey whip Douglass?
questions.explanation: Bill says he was hired to work, not to help whip Douglass; Hughes does try to help Covey.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass criticize the holiday drinking encouraged by enslavers?
choices: It makes false freedom look like drunkenness and discourages resistance.
questions.explanation: He describes holidays as a safety valve that redirects resistance and disgusts people with a distorted idea of freedom.

questions.prompt: How does Freeland differ from Covey?
choices: Better food, tools, meal time, and more straightforward behavior.
He secretly follows workers through fields.
He pays all wages to Douglass.
questions.explanation: Douglass prefers Freeland’s conditions but still wants to be his own master.

questions.prompt: What is Douglass’s central role at the Sabbath school?
questions.explanation: Henry and John Harris and more than forty learners join the school despite danger.

questions.prompt: Which description matches the planned group escape?
choices: Canoe up the Chesapeake, then follow the North Star beyond Maryland.
Ride straight to New York on a disclosed train route.
Sail to Alabama to find Hugh.
questions.explanation: The group planned to reach the head of the bay and travel north; Baltimore was their cover story.

questions.prompt: Why are passes made in William Hamilton’s name?
choices: To disguise their escape as a permitted Easter visit to Baltimore.
To prove they had already been freed.
To enter a caulking union in New Bedford.
To get into the Nantucket convention.
questions.explanation: Douglass writes the protections to reduce suspicion if questioned.

questions.prompt: What happens before the group can depart?
choices: They are arrested and taken to Easton jail.
questions.explanation: Constables seize them on the morning of their planned departure.

questions.prompt: What hurts Douglass most when the others leave jail?
choices: Having to stop a paid lecture.
questions.explanation: Their solidarity mattered deeply; he dreaded separation more than almost anything.

questions.prompt: Why is there no legal redress for the shipyard attack?
choices: No white witness will testify, and his testimony is not accepted.
All four attackers have escaped to Canada.
Hugh refuses to ask for help.
questions.explanation: Hugh seeks help from Watson, who will not issue a warrant without white testimony.

questions.prompt: What contradiction ends Chapter X?
choices: Douglass earns his wages but Hugh takes every cent.
Covey pays Douglass for resisting him.
Nathan takes Douglass’s first free earnings.
questions.explanation: Douglass contracts, works, and collects the money, but coercion makes him surrender it to Hugh.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass conceal the means of his successful escape?
choices: To protect helpers and future fugitives.
Because his book is a novel.
To hide his marriage from Anna.
questions.explanation: Publishing the methods could give enslavers information to stop other people.

questions.prompt: When does he reach New York after escaping?
questions.explanation: He reports the date and destination but deliberately withholds the route.

questions.prompt: Why does joy in New York give way to anxiety?
choices: He is isolated and fears kidnapping.
He wants to return to Covey.
He has become a wealthy shipowner.
He has lost his position as overseer.
questions.explanation: Legal and personal insecurity make apparent freedom frightening without support.

questions.prompt: Who provides shelter and recommends New Bedford?
questions.explanation: Ruggles shelters him and suggests a place where his caulking skills might provide work.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Anna Murray is correct?
choices: She is already free when she joins and marries Douglass.
She is an enslaved member of the canoe group.
questions.explanation: Anna joins him in New York; Pennington marries them on September 15, 1838.

questions.prompt: Who helps them begin life in New Bedford and suggests Douglass?
questions.explanation: Nathan pays their stage fares and proposes a name inspired by The Lady of the Lake.

questions.prompt: What surprises Douglass about New Bedford?
choices: No one works at the harbor.
questions.explanation: Its wealth challenges the claim that slavery is necessary to prosperity.

questions.prompt: Why is his first paid work in New Bedford significant?
choices: The earnings belong to him and support his household.
He must hand all earnings to Hugh.
It makes him a slave trader.
questions.explanation: Loading oil brings earnings that no enslaver can claim, though discrimination still blocks caulking work.

questions.prompt: What publication inspires his anti-slavery activity?
questions.explanation: He subscribes about four months after reaching New Bedford and follows its anti-slavery message.

questions.prompt: What event closes the main Narrative?
choices: A successful escape route explained in full.
questions.explanation: Coffin urges him to speak; the narrative closes with his work for the anti-slavery cause.

questions.prompt: What distinction is central to the Appendix?
choices: Christianity of Christ versus slaveholding religion.
questions.explanation: He explicitly defends pure, peaceable, impartial Christianity while condemning religious support for slavery.

questions.prompt: Which example shows the hypocrisy Douglass condemns?
choices: Praising family while separating enslaved families.
Paying a worker their own earnings.
questions.explanation: He tests professed values against actions toward enslaved people.

questions.prompt: Does his criticism include northern churches?
choices: Yes, when they remain in communion with slaveholders.
Yes, because he rejects all Christianity.
questions.explanation: He criticizes complicit religious bodies north and south without condemning all faith.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the closing parody?
choices: Satire that exposes pious words paired with cruel deeds.
questions.explanation: The repeated heavenly union is ironic; Douglass copies a parody attributed to a northern Methodist preacher.

questions.prompt: What does he hope the book will help accomplish?
choices: Support the trade in enslaved people.
questions.explanation: His closing pledge relies on truth, love, and justice in the cause of liberation.

questions.prompt: Which values appear in the final pledge?
questions.explanation: The ending names truth, love, and justice as the basis of his efforts.
